title: the one at every doorway
hook: an elephant-headed figure on the dashboard, by the door, at the top of the page

segments.voice: Yesterday: pranam, the bow and the blessing that comes back. Today you meet someone.

A small statue on a taxi dashboard. A picture above a shop counter. His name printed at the top of a wedding invitation, before anyone else's. Elephant head, round belly, one tusk broken. He sits wherever things start, and that's the clue to who he is.

Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. But the title that explains the doorways is Vighnaharta. Vighna, an obstacle; harta, one who removes. The remover of obstacles. That's why he's honored first: before a ceremony, a wedding, a new shop or an exam. Some people write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before they begin, and namah is the same bow as in namaste. There's a popular way of reading his body: big ears, listen more than you talk; small eyes, focus; a big belly, take in what life serves, good and hard. And the broken tusk: tradition says he wrote down the Mahabharata as the sage Vyasa dictated it, and one story says that when his pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing.
screen: `LORD OF THE GANAS.` · `VIGHNAHARTA — REMOVER OF OBSTACLES.` · `SHRI GANESHAYA NAMAH.` · `THE BROKEN TUSK.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Rest a hand on something that marks a start: a door, a laptop, a notebook. Name, once, what's in the way of the next thing you're beginning. Then breathe out and lift your hand.
Ganesha. Lord of the ganas, remover of obstacles, the one at the door. Sixth word, and the first name on your strand.
Your line: clear the road, then begin. It's why his name comes first on so many invitations. Day six.

howItsDone: Hindus honor Ganesha first at ceremonies, weddings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

story.title: the race around the world
story.text: In a story told in many versions, Shiva and Parvati offer a prize to whichever of their two sons can go around the whole world first. Kartikeya jumps on his peacock and flies off. Ganesha, round and slow, with a mouse to ride, doesn't even try to race. He walks around his parents, slowly, and bows. You two are my world, he says. He wins.
story.source: a popular story, told in different forms across India

wrong.truth: it means lord of the ganas, the attendants of Shiva. his best-known title is Vighnaharta, the remover of obstacles.

notes: The Ganesha-as-scribe episode appears in some recensions of the Mahabharata's Adi Parva and is not in the Critical Edition's main text; the script says 'tradition says'. The tusk-as-pen story is given as 'one story people tell'. Confirm.
Body symbolism (ears, eyes, belly) is given as 'a popular way of reading the body', not scripture. Confirm.
The birth and elephant-head story is deliberately held back: it is told in full on days 22–24 (Shiva Purana).
Vighnaharta transliterated as commonly written; Sanskrit vighnahartṛ. Confirm.

Cut from manuscript day 6 under the claims rule: 'walk into almost any Indian home', 'the most recognizable figure in the tradition', 'every wedding, every new business, every exam', 'the one most kids hear', 'a billion people', and 'five thousand years of people'.
Title keeps the index's 'every doorway'; the script itself says doorways, not every one.

Audit pass: cut 'not a guard who keeps you out', which a scholar would catch: Ganesha is a threshold guardian (he guards Parvati's door in the Shiva Purana story told on days 22–24) and is also Vighnakarta, who places obstacles.
